CVE-2026-116774.title: russh: peer-declared zero maximum packet size permanently stalls channel writes (silent AsyncWrite hang)
CVE-2026-116774.description: russh is a Rust SSH client and server library that includes an SSH agent protocol implementation. From 0.60.0 until 0.65.0, channel-open parsing accepts a peer-declared maximum_packet_size of zero and passes it into ChannelTx::poll_writable in russh/src/channels/io/tx.rs. The Channel::data, Channel::make_writer, and Channel::into_stream asynchronous write paths then calculate a writable size of zero and remain pending forever because window adjustments cannot satisfy a static zero packet maximum. An authenticated client can strand server writes, and a malicious server can strand client writes, allowing affected tasks, channels, and connections to accumulate without surfacing an error. This issue is fixed in version 0.65.0.

CVE-2026-119331.title: Ladybird: Missing origin-clean enforcement in CSSStyleSheet allows cross-origin CSS read and mutation
CVE-2026-119331.description: Ladybird is a truly independent web browser. CVE-2026-131179.description:
In Splunk Enterprise versions below 10.4.5, 10.2.9, 10.0.12, and 9.4.17, a user who holds the "power" Splunk role could add attacker-controlled Search Processing Language (SPL) to a shared dashboard. When another user opens the dashboard in Splunk Web, Splunk Enterprise could run the attacker-controlled SPL using the permissions of that dashboard viewer. CVE-2026-65632.title: ECDSA signature length is not validated in jose, allowing signature malleability
CVE-2026-65632.description:
The jose library accepts ECDSA (ES256, ES256K, ES384, and ES512) JWS signatures of a non-canonical length. When verifying an ECDSA signature, jose_jwk_kty_ec:verify/4 in src/jwk/jose_jwk_kty_ec.erl splits the raw signature in half by its actual byte length (split_binary(Signature, byte_size(Signature) div 2)) instead of enforcing the fixed length required by RFC 7518 §3.4, and then decodes each half with crypto:bytes_to_integer/1, which ignores leading zero bytes.

As a result, an attacker who holds one valid token can prepend leading zero bytes to each of the R and S halves to produce longer signatures that still split evenly and decode to the same (r, s) pair, so many distinct signature byte strings all verify against the same key (signature malleability). This does not allow forging new payloads or impersonating a signer, because the underlying (r, s) values are unchanged. It does defeat any security control that assumes a valid token or its signature is unique, such as…

CVE-2026-87768.title: DateTime::Lite versions before 0.8.1 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via a per-day loop when adding seconds
CVE-2026-87768.description:
DateTime::Lite versions before 0.8.1 for Perl allow CPU exhaustion via a per-day loop when adding seconds.

_normalize_leap_seconds crosses day boundaries one day at a time, so add(seconds => $n) on an object with a non-floating time zone takes about |$n|/86400 iterations, and nothing limits $n. The XS implementation and the pure-Perl fallback both have the loop.

An attacker who controls the number of seconds added can keep the process busy for as long as they choose.

CVE-2026-98878.title: irqchip/gic-v5: Immediately exec priority drop following activate
CVE-2026-98878.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

irqchip/gic-v5: Immediately exec priority drop following activate

With GICv5 an interrupt of equal or lower priority cannot be signalled
until there has been a priority drop. This is done via the GIC CDEOI
system instruction. Once this has been executed, the hardware is able
to signal the next interrupt if there is one.

As all interrupts are programmed to have the same priority, no new
interrupts can be signalled until the priority drop has happened. This
can cause issues when, for example, an interrupt remains active while
a long running process takes place, such as when injecting a physical
interrupt into a guest VM in software.

The GICv5 driver has so far done the priority drop as part of
irq_eoi(), i.e., at the same time as deactivating the interrupt. This
means that any long running process (or VM) could block incoming
interrupts, effectively causing a denial of service for all other

CVE-2026-99338.title: KVM: TDX: Enable Notify VM exit
CVE-2026-99338.description:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

KVM: TDX: Enable Notify VM exit

Enable Notify VM exit functionality for TDX guests.

Notify VM exit is an existing feature supported by KVM. Userspace can
enable Notify VM exit through KVM_CAP_X86_NOTIFY_VMEXIT when it's
reported as supported. However, KVM reports the support of this CAP just
based on the hardware capability but doesn't differentiate between VMX
and TDX. This leads to the issue that userspace can enable this cap for
TDX guests without getting an error, but the feature is not actually
enabled because KVM doesn't call the TDX module API to program the
relevant TD VMCS fields.

Enable Notify VM exit for TDX guests by:

- Invoking TDX module API calls to set NOTIFY_VM_EXITING and Notify
Window in TD VMCS. It's done in tdx_vcpu_init() where other TD VMCS
bits are set. Since TDX vCPU cannot be reset, it only needs to be
